description: Who took Robo's ice pop? Detective Cat finds the culprit: heat! Learn solid, liquid and gas, run a melt race, freeze juice, and fizz a balloon with baking soda and vinegar.

youtube.title: Melt, Freeze, Fizz! Solids, Liquids and Gases for Kids | Easy Science Experiment | Toy Box Friends
youtube.description:
Robo's ice pop is gone: only a stick and an orange puddle are left! Detective Cat takes the case.
Meet the particles in a solid, a liquid and a gas, run a melt race (sun, shade, freezer), freeze juice into a new ice pop, watch a puddle evaporate, and blow up a balloon with baking soda and vinegar.
Do the experiments with a grown-up and wear goggles. Never cap the bottle and don't taste the mixture.

scenes.title: The case of the missing ice pop

do.text: Melt, Freeze, Fizz!
My orange ice pop! I left it right here on the windowsill.
Now there's only a stick, and an orange puddle!
Someone took my ice pop! Was it you, Dog?
Not me! I was napping all day.
No one took it. But something changed it.
Detective Cat is on the case. Let's find out what.
First, a secret.
Everything is made of tiny bits called particles.
They're much too small to see, so here are giant toy ones.
In a solid, the particles are packed tight.
solid
They just wiggle in place.
So a solid keeps its shape. An ice cube, a block, an apple.
In a liquid, the particles slide past each other.
liquid
A liquid takes the shape of its cup. Water, milk, juice.
In a gas, the particles zoom far apart and fill the space!
gas
Like the air inside a balloon, or inside a bubble.
But why do they move so differently?
It's all about heat. Warmer particles move more.
Colder ones move less.
Keeps its shape? Solid! Takes the cup's shape? Liquid!
Spreads out everywhere? Gas!
So ice is a solid, but melted ice is a liquid?
Yes! The same water can be a solid, a liquid or a gas.
Solid, liquid, gas. Got it. Now, back to the case.
Detectives test their ideas. Let's have a melt race!
Three ice cubes, three plates.
Cube 1 on the sunny windowsill.
Cube 2 on the shady table.
Cube 3 in the freezer.
Which ice cube will melt first? What do you think?
I'll guard them. Nobody touches the ice!
Let's fast-forward fifteen minutes.
15 minutes
Cube 1 in the sun is mostly a puddle!
Cube 2 in the shade is half melted.
And cube 3 in the freezer is still a solid cube.
But why did it melt there, and not in the freezer?
Heat from the sun warmed the ice above zero degrees.
Zero degrees Celsius. That's thirty-two Fahrenheit.
Warm ice melts. The solid turns into a liquid!
melt
And where was the ice pop? On the sunny windowsill.
Dog didn't take it. The culprit is heat!
Sorry, Dog! You're cleared.
At home, wipe up the water after, so nobody slips.
Can we make a new ice pop? Let's freeze juice!
Pour orange juice into a plastic ice pop mould.
Leave a little space at the top.
Water grows when it freezes!
Use plastic, not glass, in the freezer.
Add a stick, and into the freezer it goes.
overnight
Good morning! Let's open the freezer.
A new ice pop!
The cold turned the liquid juice into a solid.
freeze
That's freezing!
Water freezes at zero degrees Celsius.
Fun fact: water gets a little bigger when it freezes.
That's why ice cubes float in a drink!
Can I have a lick? It's real juice!
Yes! Juice is real food. It's the only thing we eat today.
So melting goes one way, and freezing goes back.
Now a puddle mystery. Here's a little puddle of water.
Let's leave it for a whole day.
1 day
Gone! Where did it go?
The water turned into water vapour, a gas we can't see.
water vapour
It floated into the air. That's called evaporating.
evaporate
Fun fact: water is easy to find in all three states.
Ice is solid, water is liquid, and water vapour is a gas.
So the puddle didn't vanish. It just turned into a gas.
Stand up! Do the moves with the chant.
Solid stands still,
liquid likes to flow,
gas spreads out wherever it can go!
Stand stiff for solid. Sway for liquid. Tiptoe wide for gas!
Ice is solid, juice can flow,
air in a balloon has room to go!
Solid stands still, liquid likes to flow,
gas spreads out wherever it can go!
Time for the fizz lab!
With a grown-up, wear goggles
Do this with a grown-up, and wear goggles.
Goggles on!
Quack! Ready, lab partner!
First, put a tray down.
A grown-up pours vinegar into a plastic bottle.
Next, put two spoons of baking soda into a balloon.
Stretch the balloon over the neck.
Don't let the powder fall in yet!
Do it outdoors or on a tray,
so the foam is easy to clean up.
Will the balloon get bigger? What do you think?
Lift the balloon, and let the powder drop in!
Fizz! Bubbles foam up, and the balloon blows up!
But what's inside the balloon? It isn't just air.
The baking soda and vinegar make a new gas: carbon dioxide.
The gas needs space, so it fills up the balloon.
Fun fact: carbon dioxide also makes fizzy drinks fizzy!
With a grown-up, wear goggles
Safety rules: never put a cap on the bottle,
and don't taste the mixture.
Vinegar stings eyes. If it splashes, rinse with water.
Last test. Can we press undo, and change things back?
The melted ice pop? We froze the juice,
and got an ice pop back!
Melting and freezing can be undone!
And the fizz? Can we get the baking soda and vinegar back?
No! Something new was made, a gas. We can't undo the fizz.
So heating and cooling can be undone for water.
The fizz can't.
Melt, freeze, melt, freeze. Water can go back and forth.
Some changes go back. Some changes stay changed!
Challenge! Solid, liquid or gas? Shout it out!
A rock!
Solid!
Milk!
Liquid!
The air inside a ball!
Gas!
A spoon!
Solid!
Rain!
Liquid!
Water vapour in the air!
Gas!
Honey!
Liquid, a slow one!
An ice cube!
Solid!
Eight out of eight, detectives.
Quiz time! Is juice a solid, a liquid or a gas?
A liquid!
What made the ice pop melt?
Heat from the sun!
Can we undo melting? Can we undo the fizz?
Melting, yes, by freezing. The fizz, no. A new gas was made.
What filled the balloon?
A gas called carbon dioxide!
Four for four! Super scientists.
My new ice pop! Case closed!
Case closed. The culprit was heat.
Freeze some juice at home, and enjoy your own ice pop!
Try the melt race at home with a grown-up. Bye!
